analytic.title: Holistic WCRT Analysis for Global Fixed-Priority Preemptive Multiprocessor Scheduling

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Many embedded applications demand both resource efficiency and timing guarantee. However, resource sharing naturally complicates the analysis that extracts the worst-case scenario out of contention. Global Fixed-Priority (GFP) preemptive multiprocessor scheduling is one of the mainstream strategies to resolve contention on computational resources. It allows jobs of the same task to be executed on different processors, hence potentially enabling better parallelism and more efficient resource utilization. Unfortunately, its worst-case response time (WCRT) analysis is challenging. Existing approaches divide a high-priority task into three workloads, namely, carry-in workload, body workload, and carry-out workload, trying to optimize them individually. In this work, we propose a holistic WCRT analysis for GFP preemptive multiprocessor scheduling, where a task is no longer divided. Specifically, (i) we establish the tight interference scenario for the task being analyzed to find the most interfering high-priority jobs in any time interval; (ii) we obtain the starting released instant of each high-priority task's first job to determine the maximum interference from high-priority tasks' first jobs to the task being analyzed; (iii) we build the worst-case tight interference scenario for the task being analyzed by combining the tight interference scenario and the starting released instants; (iv) we prove that the WCRT of the task being analyzed can be decided by the worst-case tight interference scenario. Evaluation on schedulability shows that our proposed analysis achieves 4.2%-8.6% higher acceptance ratio in randomly generated data sets than the state-of-the-art workload division approaches.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: With the development of computing technology, multiprocessors (or multicores) are widely used in real-time embedded systems, such as robot control systems [1] and Digital Signal Processing (DSP) [2]. Many embedded applications demand both resource efficiency and timing guarantee. However, resource sharing naturally complicates the analysis that extracts the worst-case scenario out of contention. Global Fixed-Priority (GFP) multiprocessor scheduling can realize multi-task parallelism in real-time embedded systems, but it increases the difficulty of Worst-Case Response Time (WCRT) analysis. WCRT analysis means finding the maximum response time (i.e., WCRT upper bound) from the released instant to the finished instant of each task. The WCRT upper bound can determine whether the analyzed task meets its realtime requirements by comparing with the deadline [3]. The key to conducting the WCRT analysis for GFP multiprocessor scheduling is to find the critical instant, which can lead to the WCRT; however, the critical instant of a task in preemptive GFP multiprocessor scheduling has not been known based on the existing real-time analysis theories [4], such that the optimal solution cannot be proved theoretically. The above situation is one of the important difficulties in the real-time system community.

Baker [5] first proposed the problem window analysis framework to estimate a WCRT upper bound, and this framework has been applied to WCRT analysis for preemptive GFP multiprocessor scheduling [6], [7]. In the problem window analysis framework, the response process of the analyzed task is regarded as a problem window, where the workload contributed by an individual task is divided into three subpart workloads, namely, carry-in workload, body workload, and carry-out workload. The basic idea of the problem window analysis framework is below: 1) estimating the maximum workload of each high-priority task by accumulating the three sub-part workloads; 2) estimating the total interference of all high-priority tasks by accumulating the maximum workload of each high-priority task; 3) calculating the WCRT upper bound by adding the obtained total interference of all highpriority tasks and the Worst-Case Execution Time (WCET) of the currently analyzed task. That is, the WCRT analysis based on the problem window analysis framework can be regarded as the workload division approach. Considering that each subpart workload could bring pessimism, the sum of the three sub-part workloads could lead to large pessimism.

To reduce the pessimism of the workload division approach, some scholars focus on optimizing the carry-in workload estimation. Guan et al. [6] proposed a WCRT analysis approach (called GSYY1 in this paper) by limiting the number of carryin tasks. On the basis of [6], Zhou et al. [7] proposed a WCRT analysis approach through improving the carry-in workload (called ZLL 2 in this paper). However, both GSYY and ZLL merely optimize the carry-in workload estimation and ignore the fact that analysis pessimism also exists in the body workload and the carry-out workload, such that the optimization space towards tight WCRT upper bound is quite limited. It is necessary to consider new WCRT analysis approach with tight WCRT upper bound from a new perspective.

Main Contributions: To address the aforementioned technical challenges, we propose a holistic WCRT analysis for preemptive GFP multiprocessor scheduling. "Holistic" means that we no longer divide a high-priority task into carry-in workload, body workload, and carry-out workload, but treat them as a whole. We build the tight interference scenario to the analyzed task; the tight interference scenario can find the most interference high-priority jobs in any time interval. We obtain the started released instant of each high-priority task's first job; the started released instants can determine the maximum interference of high-priority tasks' first jobs to the analyzed task. We build the worst-case tight interference scenario to the analyzed task by combining the tight interference scenario and the started released instant. We prove that the WCRT of the analyzed task can be decided by the worst-case tight interference scenario. The holistic WCRT analysis demonstrates 4.2% -8.6% higher acceptance ratios than those of the mainstream workload division approaches.

div.head: A. Task Model
div.p: In this paper, we consider multiple independent and periodic real-time tasks executed on m homogeneous processors. The entire system is modeled as T = {τ 1 , τ 2 , . . . , τ n }, and n is the number of tasks. Each task is modeled as
div.formula: τ i = {C i , D i , T i },
div.p: where i is the identity of the task; for two tasks τ i and τ k , if i ¡ k, then τ i has a higher priority than τ k (i.e., the smaller the i, the higher the priority). C i is the WCET of τ i ; D i is the relative deadline of τ i ; and T i is the period of τ i . If a task τ i meets D i ≤ T i , τ i is a restrict deadline task; otherwise, τ i is an arbitrary deadline task. In particular, τ i is an implied deadline task if D i = T i . In this paper, we focus on implied deadline tasks. Table I shows a simple motivating example, where four tasks are executed on two processors, and τ 1 has the highest priority, followed by τ 2 , τ 3 and τ 4 .

div.head: B. Time Model
div.p: A task is a group of related jobs that provide a certain system function together. We use J i,x to represent the xth job of task τ i . The released instant of J i,x is denoted by r i,x and the finished instant of J i,x is denoted by f i,x . The response time R i,x of J i,x means the interval between the released instant and the finished instant, namely, we have
div.formula: R i,x = f i,x -r i,x .
div.p: The WCRT of τ i is the maximum value among all response time of its jobs and is denoted as R i , namely, we have
div.formula: R i = max x⩾1 R i,x .
div.p: Assume that we aim to analyze the WCRT of τ 4 on two processors; since the WCRT analysis in preemptive GFP scheduling is performed in the order of priority from high to low, we have known the WCRTs of all high-priority tasks (i.e., τ 1 , τ 2 , and τ 3 ) of τ 4 by using GSYY [6], ZLL [7], or our proposed NEW approach (i.e., the holistic approach). In other words, three WCRT analysis approaches can obtain the same WCRT for τ 1 as well as τ 2 and τ 3 . Table I shows that the WCRTs of τ 1 , τ 2 , and τ 3 are 4, 4, and 11, respectively. In the following section, we will analyze the WCRT of τ 4 using our proposed NEW approach. At the end of the next section, we will see that the WCRT values of τ 4 obtained by the three approaches are different.

div.head: III. HOLISTIC WCRT ANALYSIS
div.p: Unlike GSYY [6] and ZLL [7], our holistic analysis no longer divides each high-priority task into carry-in workload, body workload, and carry-out workload.

div.head: C. Started Released Instant to the Analyzed Task
div.p: Considering that the tight interference scenario does not necessarily lead to the WCRT upper bound of τ k according to Theorem 2, we need to make some adjustments to the released instants of some high-priority tasks.

Definition 3. Started released instant: The started released instant is defined as the released instant of the analyzed task's first job or each high-priority task's first job; For the analyzed task, its started released instant is 0; For each high-priority task, its started released instant is not necessarily 0.

In Fig. 3, the started released instants of the analyzed task (i.e., τ 4 ) and high-priority tasks (i.e., τ 1 , τ 2 , and τ 3 ) are all 0. In this case, the interference of the first jobs of high-priority tasks to τ 4 is 4 (i.e., the interference in the time interval of [0,4]). In other words, the start execution instant of τ 4 is not the latest. To obtain the maximum interference of the first jobs of high-priority tasks to τ k , the first jobs of high-priority tasks cannot be released simultaneously at instant 0, but the released instants of partial high-priority tasks need to be postponed to larger instants.

Principle 1. The first jobs of high-priority tasks are executed in the descending order of WCETs (if the WCET of the jobs are equal, these jobs are executed in the descending order of priority values, namely, in the ascending order of priority).

Theorem 3. Executing the first job of all high-priority tasks according to Principle 1 can delay the start execution time of τ k to the greatest extent, resulting in the maximum interference value of τ k by the first job of all high-priority tasks.

Proof. It can be seen from principle 1 that the first jobs of all high-priority tasks are executed from time 0 in the descending order of WCET. In other words, the larger the WCET, the earlier the first job of the high-priority task is executed, and the greater the interference value contributed by the first job of the high-priority task. The execution time of τ k depends on the idle situation of each processor when the execution of the first job of all high-priority tasks is completed. In other words, in order to ensure full utilization of each processor, τ k will be scheduled to start execution at the nearest idle time. Therefore, when the first job of the high priority task with a larger WCET is executed first, the more time is occupied on the processor. According to the principle of addition and accumulation, compared with other execution orders, the execution order based on principle 1 will accumulate more execution time on each processor, that is, the first jobs of all high-priority tasks will lead to more interference value on τ k . ■ For instance, when analyzing the WCRT of τ 4 , different execution orders of the first jobs of high-priority tasks (i.e., τ 1 , τ 2 and τ 3 ) will cause different interference situations on τ 4 .

(1) In Fig. 4, J 1,1 , J 2,1 , and J 3,1 are executed in order of priority from high to low. The first jobs of all high-priority tasks generate an interference value of 4 for J 4,1 , causing J 4,1 to start execution at the instant of 4.
(2) In Fig. 5, J 3,1 , J 2,1 , and J 1,1 are executed in descending order of WCET; in this way, the interference value of the first jobs of all high-priority tasks to J 4,1 is 7.

The interference value in Fig. 5 is larger than that in Fig. 4, such that J 4,1 can be executed at a later instant. Fig. 5: The first jobs of high-priority tasks are executed in order of WCET from large to small, namely, J3,1, J2,1, and J1,1.

Definition 5. Worst-case tight interference scenario: The worst-case tight interference scenario to τ k happens when high-priority tasks are released in terms of individual worstcase tight interference flows.
Theorem 4. The worst-case tight interference scenario leads to the WCRT upper bound of τ k .
Proof. We prove the theorem from two aspects.

(1) On one hand, Principle 1 determines the started released instant of each high-priority task's first job, thereby ensuring that τ k is interfered with the maximum delay and delaying the start execution instant of τ k ; by this treatment, we can prevent the situation that τ k can be executed after interfered by the high-priority tasks' first jobs to the greatest extent.

(2) On the other hand, the subsequent jobs (except for the first job) of each high-priority task are released according to Principle 2; by this treatment, we can find the most interference jobs in any time interval according to Theorem 1.

Through the above 2 treatments, the response time obtained under the worst-case tight interference scenario is larger than or equal to all the real response time values. That is, the WCRT upper bound of the analyzed task is decided by the worst-case tight interference scenario. ■ Fig. 6 shows that high-priority tasks τ 2 and τ 3 are still released simultaneously at instant 0 according to the individual tight interference flows. However, τ 1 is released according to the tight interference flow with Principle 1. Different from Fig. 3 that only the first jobs of τ 1 and τ 2 cause interference to τ 4 , Fig. 6 shows that the first jobs of all three high-priority tasks τ 1 , τ 2 , and τ 3 cause interference to τ 4 . The response time of τ 4 in Fig. 6 is calculated as 19, which is a safe WCRT upper bound. Finally, the WCRT upper bounds of τ 4 obtained by GSYY, ZLL, and NEW are shown in Table II. As we can see from Table II, the WCRTs obtained by NEW has the minimum value of 19 among three approaches. Note that 19 is an unreachable WCRT because our approach is still pessimistic but is tighter than the workload division approaches.

div.head: IV. EXPERIMENTAL EVALUATION
div.p: We adopt the same way as [6], [7] to generate random data sets, then we perform experiments based on these data sets. The approaches compared with the proposed WCRT analysis approach are GSYY [6] and ZLL [7]. The evaluation metric is the acceptance ratio. Similar to [6], [7], the deadline of each task τ i is set to be an implicit deadline (i.e., D i = T i ), whereas T i is uniformly distributed in [2,100]. U i is the utilization of each task τ i , namely, U i = Ci Ti . U i is set to be uniformly distributed in (0, 0.125], (0, 0.25], (0, 0.5], respectively. C i is generated by C i = T i ×U i . The number of processors is set to vary from 2 to 10. As for task priorities, we assign the priority to each task according to the rate monotonic scheme. Figs. 789show the acceptance ratio obtained by GSYY, ZLL, and NEW under different task utilization ranges. Based on the same data set generation approach as [6], [7], when the total utilization of all tasks is equal to or larger than the number of processors, the random task is stopped to generate and the number of the data set is determined. Therefore, the number of tasks generated by the task utilization range (0, 0.125] is the largest, followed by the range of (0, 0.25] and (0, 0.5]. In other words, we analyze the acceptance ratio obtained by GSYY, ZLL, and NEW under different numbers on three different scale data sets.

In general, the acceptance ratio obtained by NEW is higher than GSYY and ZLL in all cases, as shown in Figs. 789. Moreover, the changing trend of the acceptance ratio is similar. We take Fig. 7 as an example for detailed analysis.

(1) The acceptance ratio decreases as the number of processors increases by using all approaches; the results reflect that NEW follows the same pattern (i.e., acceptance ratio decreases with the increase of the number of processors) as GSYY and ZLL.

(2) The acceptance ratio obtained by NEW is the largest in all cases. That is, NEW shows a stable advantage compared to GSYY and ZLL in all cases. Using NEW to perform WCRT analysis can obtain higher acceptance ratios and better guarantee the real-time performance of the system.

To analyze the improvement effect of acceptance ratio, we calculate the increase of acceptance ratio between NEW and ZLL (i.e., AR(NEW) -AR(ZLL)) based on different task utilization ranges in Table III.

(1) Maximum increase means the maximum increase value among all values under a given task utilization range. For example, the value 8.6% in Table III is the maximum increase value among all increase values based on the data set with utilization range of (0, 0.125].
(2) From Table III, we can see the increase of acceptance ratio is basically in the range of (4.2%, 8.6%), that is, NEW has increased the acceptance ratio by 4.2% to 8.6% compared with ZLL.

(3) When the task utilization range is (0, 0.125], the average increase is the largest among three task utilization ranges. This reflects that the larger the number of tasks, the better the improvement effect of the acceptance ratio.

In summary, our proposed holistic WCRT analysis approach performs better than existing mainstream approaches GSYY and ZLL in terms of acceptance ratio, especially when the number of tasks is relatively large. In other words, NEW is also suitable for large-scale task systems.

div.head: V. CONCLUSION
div.p: To reduce the pessimism of WCRT analysis when using the workload division approach in preemptive GFP multiprocessor scheduling, a holistic WCRT analysis approach is proposed in this paper. The holistic approach can obtain safe and tight WCRT upper bounds by building worst-case tight interference scenario. The holistic approach can obtain higher acceptance ratios than the mainstream workload division approaches. The holistic approach provides a new WCRT analysis technical solution and promotes the development of real-time multiprocessor scheduling theory. The holistic approach is still a pessimistic WCRT analysis approach, but it has taken an important step forward in reducing pessimism.
